name: Maasai Nborr Collar
description: The nborr is the flat beaded collar worn by Maasai women and, on ceremonial occasions, by young men (moran) of Kenya and Tanzania. Built on a base of hide or wire and covered with dense rows of tiny glass beads, the collar forms a broad crescent that lies across the chest and shoulders. The colour combinations are not arbitrary: red stands for the cattle that are the heart of Maasai life, white for milk and peace, and the patterns signal the age-set, clan, and status of the wearer. Beaded ornaments are made by women, who learn the craft from their mothers, and whose beadwork circulates in the exchanges that build family alliances. The nborr is worn at dances, initiations, and the celebrations that mark the passage of the age-sets. Maasai beadwork has also become an economic mainstay, with women's cooperatives selling collars and jewellery to the wider market.

name: Maasai Rungu Club
description: The rungu is a short throwing club of the Maasai, a knobbed head on a tapering wooden shaft that herders and warriors carry as they move with their cattle. In the past the rungu was a practical weapon for defending livestock against predators and for settling disputes, thrown with a spin that drove the heavy knob home with force. Today it is still carried, but its main work is ceremonial and social: elders raise the rungu to command attention at meetings, and the club is a badge of authority for spokesmen and age-set leaders. Decorated rungu, carved with rings and bands and sometimes tipped with metal, are made for chiefs and for the tourist market. The word has passed into the region's popular culture, and the rungu remains the most recognisable symbol of Maasai leadership.

name: Maasai Shuka Cloth
era: Contemporary, evolving from traditional hide cloth
description: The shuka is the checked cloth, usually in shades of red, that Maasai wrap around the body as a toga-like garment, a dress so distinctive it has become the visual signature of the Maasai in Kenya and Tanzania. Red is the colour of cattle blood and of the warrior ideal, and the bold plaid stands out in the savannah where the herds graze. The shuka replaced the older dress of hides and skins during the twentieth century, when imported cotton cloth spread through the region, and its adoption shows how a modern commodity was absorbed into Maasai identity. Different communities favour different colour families, and the way the cloth is folded and worn, over one shoulder, around the waist, or across the mouth of a herder sheltering from dust, varies with occasion and age-set. Factories in the region now print shuka cloth in bulk, and the checked patterns are also worn far beyond the Maasai as a mark of East African style.

name: Ngoma Drum (Swahili Coast)
description: The ngoma is the wooden drum of the Swahili coast of Tanzania and Kenya, built as a barrel or goblet with a hide head and played in the ensembles that accompany weddings, dances, and life-cycle rites. In Swahili the word ngoma covers drum, dance, and festivity together, and the drumming groups of the coast keep a repertory of named rhythms passed down through families. Ngoma also reaches into the spirit world: in the ceremonies of the pepo, the capricious spirits of the coast, drumming summons the spirits so that they may be spoken to and soothed, and drummers are chosen for their knowledge of the right rhythm for each spirit. Coastal ensembles combine drums of several sizes and pitches, and the master drummer leads with improvised phrases while the group holds the pattern. The tradition is alive today in the taarab and dansi scenes as well as in the village ceremonies where the drums still call the community together.

name: Makonde Shetani Figure
description: The shetani carvings of the Makonde are dark hardwood figures of contorted, expressive spirits, carved from the ebony-like mpingo of the Tanzanian and Mozambican coast. Beginning in the 1950s, carvers turned from ancestor figures to the shetani, capricious bush and ancestral spirits, twisting human and animal forms into elongated, agonised, or playful shapes that seem to catch a spirit mid-transformation. Each carving is original, the forms said to be revealed to the carver in dreams, and the pieces are exhibited as art as much as ritual objects. The word shetani, from the Arabic for 'evil spirit', entered Swahili through Islam, but the figures draw on older Makonde beliefs about the dark forest and its inhabitants. Shetani carving has become one of the most recognisable genres of contemporary African art, sold from Dar es Salaam to international galleries. The tradition also carries the older meaning of the spirits themselves, who are remembered as crowding the Makonde homeland on both sides of the border.

name: Zanzibar Dhow
description: The dhow (jahazi) of Zanzibar is a lateen-sailed wooden vessel built on the Swahili coast for fishing, cargo, and the trade that rode the monsoons across the Indian Ocean. Hulls were traditionally sewn with coconut-coir fibre and caulked, and the ships carried ivory, cloves, mangrove poles, and grain between East Africa, Arabia, and India. The pattern of the monsoons set the rhythm of the whole coast: dhows sailed out on the kusi winds and returned with the kaskazi, and captains timed their passages by the stars. Seafaring was wrapped in maritime belief, and sailors made offerings and prayers to win the favour of the pepo, the sea spirits who were believed to command wind and water. The same trade carried the brasswork, textiles, and coral-stone architecture that shaped the coastal towns. Today traditional dhows still fish the Zanzibar channel, and the wooden dhow industry survives alongside modern vessels.

name: Buganda Royal Drum (Mujaguzo)
description: The mujaguzo are the royal drums of the Buganda kingdom of Uganda, a set of tuned drums kept in a sacred drum house and regarded as the spiritual king of the kingdom. Ganda tradition holds that Buganda has two rulers, the human kabaka and the drums, which never die, and the drums are sounded to announce the birth of a prince, the death of a kabaka, the call to war, and the great ceremonies of state. The principal drum, Kawulugumu, is the 'king among drums', and at a coronation the new kabaka must first visit the drum house, tighten its hide, and strike it to take up his rule; its companion Namanyonyi is spoken of as its wife. The drums are kept suspended above the ground and are smeared with ghee and beer in ritual care, guarded by custodians of the Butiko clan. When the kingdom was abolished in 1966 the drums were hidden away and survived, and they were brought out again for the coronation of 1993. The royal drum tradition remains a living institution of the kabaka's court.

name: Baganda Barkcloth (Olubugo)
material: Beaten inner bark of the mutuba fig tree
description: Olubugo is the barkcloth of the Baganda of Uganda, made by stripping the inner bark of the mutuba fig tree and beating it with wooden mallets until it becomes a soft, pliable, chestnut-brown textile. The craft is usually practised by men, who peel the bark in the wet season and beat it on a log, folding and turning the sheet until it reaches the desired fineness, and a single tree can be harvested again and again. In the Buganda kingdom, barkcloth was the dress of kings and chiefs, worn in layers that grew thicker with rank, and it was also used in burial, wrapping the dead and lining the royal tombs of Kasubi. Because it belonged to the court and the ancestors, the cloth carries sacred associations, and it is still worn and laid out at funerals and important rituals. UNESCO inscribed Baganda barkcloth-making on the list of intangible cultural heritage in 2005, and makers in the Kampala region produce cloth for ceremony and for the contemporary art and fashion markets alike.
source: Ganda barkcloth tradition; UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage

name: Ethiopian Processional Cross
description: Ethiopian processional crosses are tall brass, silver, or bronze crosses carried on staffs before the clergy during the liturgy of the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. Each cross is unique, built from a dense tracery of openwork that varies with the workshop and the region; the arms are set in a frame that may be square, round, or diamond-shaped, and the patterns are filled with small figurative and geometric motifs. The cross is both instrument and image: it is held over the congregation as a blessing, kissed by the faithful, and its openwork is understood to evoke the Tree of Life and the victory of Christ. Processional crosses accompany the tabot at outdoor festivals such as the Meskel finding of the True Cross, when the square cross itself stands at the centre of the bonfire ceremony. Silver crosses were made for the great monasteries of Lalibela and Axum, while brass crosses were the common liturgical object of every church. Related hand crosses, carried by every priest, share the same design language.

name: Jebena Coffee Pot
description: The jebena is the round, clay coffee pot of Ethiopia, with a narrow neck, a round belly, and a small spout, fired without glaze and used in the country's coffee ceremony (bunna). In the ceremony, green beans are roasted in a pan over coals, ground, and boiled three times in the jebena, and the pot sits on a bed of fresh grass while incense burns beside it. The first brew, abol, is the strongest and most honoured; the second and third rounds, tona and baraka, follow as the gathering lingers. Pouring from the high-necked pot without spilling is a skill, and the tiny cups are filled from a single unbroken stream. The jebena is central to hospitality: hosting the ceremony is a daily ritual of friendship and community, and the coffee is shared with anyone who arrives. Modern jebena are also made in metal and glazed ceramic, but the hand-built clay pot remains the heart of the tradition.

name: Ethiopian Ketab Protective Scroll
material: Parchment, ink, leather or cloth cover
powers: Worn or hung to ward off evil spirits, illness, and the harm attributed to buda.
description: Ketab are protective prayer scrolls of the Ethiopian Orthodox tradition, strips of parchment inscribed with prayers, sacred names, and devotional images, then rolled and worn or hung as amulets. They are written by debtera, the church's trained scholars, and by diviners, who combine liturgical texts with protective formulae in Ge'ez. The scrolls guard the wearer against evil spirits, illness, the evil eye, and the harm that is believed to come from buda, the people accused of possessing the evil eye. A scroll's shape follows its purpose: some are narrow strips folded into a leather case for wearing round the neck, while others are long, illustrated rolls made for the sick to keep at home. The images, crosses, eyes, saints, and the Archangel Michael on his horse, echo church painting in miniature. Ketab are still commissioned today, keeping alive a manuscript tradition that reaches back centuries.
source: Ethiopian magical scroll tradition; scholarly studies (J. Mercier)

name: Kalinga Royal Drum
description: The Kalinga was the most sacred drum of the Rwandan court, the principal of the four royal drums that together stood for the kingship of the mwami. Kept in a sacred house where a fire burned day and night, the drum was never allowed to touch the ground and was rubbed with bull's blood and herbs to renew its power. According to oral tradition the Kalinga reached the court with the seventeenth-century king Ruganzu II Ndori, and it travelled with the king on campaign, acquiring personal names as if it were a living ruler. The Kalinga stood for the male principle and the king, its companion drum for the queen mother, and Rwandans said 'he is king who has the drums': beating it at coronations, harvests, and victories affirmed the dynasty's authority. After the monarchy was abolished in the early 1960s the royal drums vanished from public sight, and no trace of the originals has been found, though the drums live on in the country's drumming tradition and in the re-created court dances of the Intore.

name: Somali Dabqaad Incense Burner
description: The dabqaad is the incense burner of Somali homes, a small clay or soapstone bowl raised on short legs and covered by a perforated lid from which the smoke of frankincense and myrrh rises. Somalia sits at the eastern end of the ancient incense lands, and the gums burned in the dabqaad were the same resins traded to Egypt, Rome, and the Gulf for thousands of years. In daily use the burner perfumes the house, and a lit dabqaad is placed near the door to welcome guests, to scent the rooms after cooking, and to sweeten the air at weddings and religious gatherings. The perforated lid lets the smoke rise in a fine plume, and the burner is carried from room to room by the women of the household. The dabqaad keeps the Horn of Africa's incense culture alive in domestic form, linking modern Somali life to one of the oldest trades in the world.

name: Mahafaly Aloalo Funerary Post
description: The aloalo are the carved funerary posts of the Mahafaly people of southwestern Madagascar, tall wooden stelae that stand on the stone tombs of chiefs and wealthy families. The name comes from alo, 'intermediary' or 'messenger', and the posts are believed to help the dead cross into the community of the ancestors. A classic aloalo rises through a column of openwork geometric shapes, crescents and circles often read as the phases of the moon, to a finial carved as a human figure, a zebu, or a bird such as the cattle egret, while the horns of zebu sacrificed at the funeral are arranged at the tomb's base. The zebu, the measure of wealth in the region, is carved again and again, and recent aloalo add motifs such as bicycles, aeroplanes, and scenes from the deceased's life. Only commissioned carvers make aloalo, which were once the right of royalty alone. The posts have become an emblem of Madagascar, and the Mahafaly tomb country is a candidate for the World Heritage list.
